name: Abermenai
summary: The youngest of the proving fields, a drowned shore at the mouth of the Menai around Dun Abermenai, for soldiers of 15 to 19.

facts.text: Abermenai is the battleground for levels 15 to 19 (region 253); level is the only limit in Offline DAoC.
Its central keep is Dun Abermenai; an Albion, a Midgard and a Hibernia portal keep stand at the same three places as in the other battlegrounds.
Dun Abermenai starts neutral in the release world.
Thidranki, Murdaigean and Caledonia were the classic battlegrounds; Abermenai came with patch 1.62 (June 2003).

Its monsters are boogey spawn, forlorn spectres, clicking beetles, large rats and forest cats (levels 13-19); renegade guardians, rangers and commanders (22) hold Dun Abermenai under Renegade Chieftain Abermenai (29).

facts.text: Abermenai Point is a real headland on the Menai Strait in Wales; Welsh "aber" means a river mouth or estuary. The battleground's name reads as Welsh, to verify that Mythic meant the place.

In the Second Branch of the Mabinogi the king's daughter sails from Aber Menei with thirteen ships to marry the king of Ireland; in the Fourth Branch Gwydion walks the boy without a name along the shore toward Aber Menei and makes a boat of sedge and seaweed (Guest's translation).
Anglesey's English name comes from the Old Norse Ongulsey, "Ongull's island"; the Welsh call the old hut circles of the island Cytiau'r Gwyddelod, "the Irishmen's huts".
The thirteen ships, the boy without a name, the dun of the west, Ongul's isle, the spectres facing the water and Brother Deiniol's gate book are Living Server lore.

story:
Abermenai is the youngest of the fields, and the realms opened it last, for the youngest of their own. In the first summers they sent their fifteens to Thidranki among soldiers five years older and counted what came of it, and then each realm found the way open to a fourth field: a shore of sand and reed where a river runs out into a grey strait.

All three realms have a name on it. Abermenai is Albion's word, the old tongue of the west for the mouth of the Menai, and Albion remembers that a king's daughter once sailed from that shore with thirteen ships to make a peace with Hibernia, and that the peace ended in a war which left seven men of the Island alive. Dun is Hibernia's word, and Hibernia says its people raised the fort above the ford when the shore was theirs. Midgard's skalds call the island by a northern name and claim only to have burned it once, which they hold to be a kind of title.

The sea came in over the flats one winter and went out again, and the forlorn spectres walk there still, grey and slow, and face the water when they weep. Boogeys hunt in the reeds. Renegades hold Dun Abermenai under a chieftain who has taken its name.

It is the field every soldier remembers, because for most of them it was the first.
legend: Abermenai is the 15-19 battleground and, for most characters, the first RvR they see. Dun Abermenai in the middle is held by renegades (guardians, rangers and commanders at 22) under Renegade Chieftain Abermenai at 29, so a group of fifteens needs to be a real group to take it. The flats are full of boogey spawn and forlorn spectres that attack anyone, so do not drag a fight through them. The portal keeps are safe ground and everything between them is not. Players call it the beach and grumble about level 19s in full crafted armour.

loremaster.intro: Abermenai, the drowned shore, the youngest of the proving fields. Ask me of [Dun Abermenai], of the [spectres] on the flats or the [boogeys] in the reeds.

topics.dun abermenai: A fort above the ford, raised by the people of the west and rebuilt in stone since by somebody nobody names. Renegades hold it under a chieftain who has taken its name, as the renegade chieftains of the fields do.
topics.spectres: Grey shapes on the flats, slow and weeping, that go toward any light and turn on whoever carries it. They always face the water. The shore-folk said they were the drowned of the winter the sea came in. The young who serve there say they are waiting for a ship.
topics.boogeys: Small hungry things of the reeds, older than the [spectres]. The shore-folk used them to keep their children near the fire, and the children who stayed near it grew up.

book.title: The Gate Book of Abermenai, kept by Brother Deiniol, chaplain at Albion's gate
pages: I was sent to keep Albion's gate at Abermenai in the summer it was opened, and to pray over any of our young who came back to it dead, and in the first week I found there was nobody to pray over. They go down the slope at dusk, twelve or twenty together, in mail that was their fathers' and does not fit them, and some of them fall on the flats or under the walls of the old fort. They do not stay fallen. They come to themselves on the stones of our gate, cold as the sea and whole, and sit up, and look about them for their swords.

From the second week I kept this book. I wrote in it each one who woke at the gate, and the first words each one spoke. I had meant to record the mercy of God, and I have recorded instead a great many young people asking for their swords, and for water, and for a particular friend, and some of them for their mothers, though seldom aloud. The mothers are mostly at the other end of the way, by the teleporters in town. Nobody sends them home. I asked the Knight Commander why not, and he said that nobody had asked him to.

One question is in this book more often than all the others together. They ask whether the day was won. The Academy has since asked me what I told them, and the answer is that I told them I did not know, which was the truth, because the keep cannot be seen from the gate. That is the whole of what I learned at Abermenai, and I set it down for whoever keeps the gate after me. From the gate you never see how it went. You see only that they come back, and it is enough to be going on with.

albion.story: Albion tells Abermenai as its own shore. The name is in Albion's old tongue, the mouth of the Menai, and two of Albion's oldest stories begin there: the king's daughter who sailed from it with thirteen ships to make a peace with Hibernia, and the boy without a name whom Gwydion walked along it to win him one. Albion's chaplains kept its gate in the first summer, and Brother Deiniol's gate book is read to every muster of squires on the night they come home from their first field, and never on the night before.

loremaster.intro: Abermenai is the youngest of the proving fields, a shore of sand and reed where a river runs out into the strait, and the name is ours: in the old tongue of the west it means the mouth of the Menai. Two old stories belong to that shore, the [thirteen ships] and the [boy without a name]. The fort above the ford is [Dun Abermenai]; the flats belong to the [spectres] and the reeds to the [boogeys].

topics.thirteen ships: In the old days a king's daughter of the Island went down to that shore and sailed from it with thirteen ships to marry the king of Hibernia, and so make a peace between two lands. She bore him a son. At the feast that was to seal the peace her own half-brother threw the child into the fire, and the war that came of it left seven men of the Island alive and Hibernia empty but for five women. She came home with the seven, and her heart broke on the shore. Albion does not tell the story to its squires before they go to Abermenai. It tells them afterward.
topics.boy without a name: His mother laid it on him that he should have no name until she gave him one, and she would not give it. So Gwydion, who had raised him, walked him down the shore toward Aber Menai, and there made a boat of sedge and seaweed, and sailed it to her castle in the guise of a shoemaker, and tricked her into naming the boy herself. Gwydion left a wood full of trees standing in battle order to see to it, which is another story, and belongs to Caledonia. Of all the stories of that shore it is the only one that ends well, and Albion tells it often for that reason.

midgard.story: Midgard does not much care whose word Abermenai is. The skalds call the island it lies on Ongul's isle, after a sea-king of Midgard who came there with three ships and burned what he found, and that is the whole of Midgard's claim. Midgard's young go to the drowned shore as the others do, and come back from it as the others do, and the skalds say that the beach has taught more of them to hold a line than any jarl.

loremaster.intro: Abermenai. The youngest of the proving fields, and a beach. The Albions named the river mouth and the Hibernians named the fort, and both will tell you the field is theirs. Ask me of [Ongul's isle] and you will hear Midgard's claim, which is shorter. The keep above the ford is [Dun Abermenai]. Mind the [spectres]; they mind nobody.

topics.ongul's isle: The skalds call the island Abermenai lies on Ongul's isle, after a sea-king of ours who came there with three ships and burned it. That is the whole of Midgard's claim. The skalds count it a good one, since nobody can say that Ongul did not do it, and they point out that the other two claims rest on old words, which anyone may use.

hibernia.story: Hibernia tells Abermenai as a shore that was its own before Albion had a name to put on it. People of the west lived there in round houses of stone and raised the dun above the ford to keep the crossing; Albion's chroniclers say their kings drove them off, and Hibernia's say they went home when they had a mind to. The stones of their houses are under the dunes yet, and the young of Hibernia who serve at the drowned shore are told so on their first night.

loremaster.intro: Abermenai, the drowned shore, the youngest of the proving fields. The Albions will tell you the name is theirs, and so it is, the half of it. The other half is [the dun], and that half is ours. Out on the flats are the [spectres], and in the reeds the [boogeys], and above the ford is [Dun Abermenai], with a renegade in it wearing its name.

topics.the dun: Long before there was an Albion to argue with, there were people of the west living on that shore, in round houses of stone, and they raised the dun above the ford to keep the crossing. The Albions' chroniclers say their kings drove them off it. Our own say they went home when they had a mind to, and left the dun standing to show they had been there. Their stones are under the dunes yet, and the Albions have a name for them in their own tongue that means the huts of the Gaels. They have never once thought to call them anything else.
